title: US Tells Allies: Pick a Side in the AI Race With China
excerpt: A leaked State Department letter warns 35 countries they cannot join both Washington's Pax Silica AI coalition and Beijing's rival framework.
body:
• The US is preparing to tell 35 countries they must choose between Washington's AI coalition and Beijing's competing framework, according to a draft State Department letter reviewed by Reuters.
  • Washington launched Pax Silica in 2025 to secure supply chains for AI models, semiconductors, and critical minerals.
  • Kazakhstan is the only country known to have joined both the US and Chinese AI initiatives, triggering the ultimatum.
  • China's Xi Jinping launched a rival "World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization" in July, promoting open-weight AI models.

The United States is preparing to force a binary choice on dozens of countries in the escalating AI race with China. A draft State Department letter, reviewed by Reuters, warns 35 signatories of a US "AI Opportunity Statement" that they will be excluded from Washington's AI coalition if they simultaneously sign up for Beijing's competing framework.

Pax Silica: Washington's AI Alliance

The ultimatum centers on Pax Silica, an initiative Washington launched in 2025 to secure supply chains for AI models, semiconductors, and the critical minerals that power them. About two dozen countries have joined, including close US allies Japan, Australia, and South Korea.

The draft letter, prepared by the State Department and addressed to the 35 signatories — which include Pax Silica members and other countries that have expressed interest in aligning AI cooperation with Washington — makes the stakes explicit.

"To be part of everything is to be part of nothing. Signature of the Pax Silica Declaration is not merely a membership subscription, but a commitment."

— US State Department draft letter

"It cannot be held alongside membership in duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with our own," the letter states, without specifically naming China.

Kazakhstan Triggered the Alarm

The catalyst was Kazakhstan. The Central Asian nation, a key potential source of critical minerals, is the only country known to have joined both the US-led Pax Silica framework and China's rival initiative, setting off alarm bells in Washington.

The US touted Kazakhstan in June as the first country in Central Asia to join Pax Silica, highlighting its significant reserves of critical minerals. But Astana's simultaneous engagement with Beijing's framework undercut the exclusivity Washington was building.

"You can't have it both ways," a US official told Reuters, speaking anonymously given ongoing internal discussions.

China's Counter-Move

In July, Chinese President Xi Jinping launched the "World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization," promoting China's open-weight AI technology as a direct challenge to US influence over the sector. The move came as Chinese open-weight models have made rapid gains against proprietary systems from US companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.

China's embassy in Washington pushed back against the US approach. "Such actions will only stifle global AI advances and serve no one's interests," an embassy spokesperson said.

Beijing is simultaneously weighing restrictions on overseas access to some of China's leading AI models, highlighting the tension between its push for global AI influence and its national security agenda.

What's at Stake

The Pax Silica agreement aims to push US allies and partners toward joint projects and export controls, ultimately reducing reliance on adversaries for critical minerals, AI models, and semiconductor chips. Members get access to shared investment opportunities in AI-related projects.

For countries caught in the middle, the choice is consequential. China has used its near-monopolies over critical minerals as a retaliatory weapon in the tariff war launched by President Trump, who has ramped up US efforts to source minerals domestically and from allies.

"It's difficult to see how a country can credibly position themselves as trusted partners in one technology ecosystem while simultaneously signing up for an initiative designed by China to advance a competing vision for AI."

— US official speaking to Reuters

Reuters could not determine when the US intends to send the letter or whether it might be amended before sending. The State Department declined to comment on "purportedly leaked internal documents."

Implications for India

The forced choice carries particular weight for India, which has maintained strategic technology relationships with both Washington and Beijing while pursuing its own AI ambitions. New Delhi has not joined either framework but has deepened semiconductor cooperation with the US through bilateral agreements. The ultimatum could pressure India to formalize its alignment — or risk being left out of preferential access to US AI infrastructure and chip technology.
